strengths: The paper studies an important and practically relevant question: whether neural operators remain accurate when evaluated at discretizations different from those used during training.
The decomposition into resolution interpolation and frequency-information extrapolation is conceptually useful, and the spectral diagnostics reveal failure modes that aggregate MSE can obscure.
Experiments cover three PDE datasets with different dimensionality and dynamics, multiple train/test resolutions, and comparisons to FNO, CNO, CROP, and physics-informed training.
Multi-resolution training is simple and practically useful; the results suggest that including even modest high-resolution coverage can improve robustness across resolutions.
The appendix contains extensive additional spectra, resolution matrices, and hyperparameter-search information.
weaknesses: The central claim conflates discretization invariance with extrapolation to unseen frequency content. A neural operator representing the same band-limited function on a finer grid is distinct from predicting physical modes absent from all training observations. Failure on the latter is largely expected and does not by itself refute standard discretization-invariance or zero-shot-resolution claims.

Several key results are not statistically reliable: the paper reports no repeated runs, uncertainty intervals, or seed sensitivity. This is especially serious for Navier–Stokes, where some models have enormous errors even at or near their training resolution, indicating optimization failures rather than a clean resolution-shift effect.

Hyperparameters are tuned at only one resolution per dataset and then reused elsewhere. Physics-informed models sometimes fail even in-distribution, and a CNO configuration does not converge, so conclusions that these methods cannot remedy resolution shift are not supported by competitive implementations.

The normalized spectral-residual metric is insufficiently defined. Normalizing by very small or filtered-out ground-truth spectral energy can magnify negligible high-frequency artifacts by orders of magnitude, while the corresponding Darcy and Burgers MSE differences are sometimes modest.

The proposed remedy has limited novelty: training on the test-domain resolutions predictably improves performance. Comparisons do not cleanly control total samples, optimization steps, pixel budget, or wall-clock compute, so the claimed low computational overhead is not established quantitatively.

Important reproducibility details are missing, including dataset sizes and splits, precise filtering/downsampling procedures, complete architecture settings, seed information, and released code; the manuscript's code field is blank.
The multi-resolution mixture specification appears erroneous or ambiguous: one stated tuple, (0.9, 0.5, 0.3, 0.2), does not form proportions because it sums to 1.9.

The conclusions are broader than the evidence, which focuses primarily on one FNO implementation and three benchmark PDEs. Claims about machine-learned operators generally require more architectures, stronger controlled baselines, and a clearer separation of discretization error from genuinely out-of-distribution physics.

strengths: The paper studies a practically important question: whether neural operators remain accurate when evaluated at discretizations different from those used for training.
The decomposition into resolution interpolation and frequency-information extrapolation is conceptually useful and helps organize the empirical analysis.

The evaluation spans three PDE datasets, several train/test resolutions, spectral diagnostics, MSE measurements, qualitative predictions, physics-informed objectives, band-limited methods, and a maximum-modes ablation.
The experiments provide useful evidence that naive FNO deployment across resolutions can produce severe artifacts, particularly for Navier–Stokes rollouts.
Mixed-resolution training is simple and practically relevant, and the experiments suggest that including some high-resolution examples can improve robustness across tested grids.
weaknesses: The central claims substantially overreach the evidence. Most of the diagnosis concerns one architecture, FNO, yet the paper repeatedly draws conclusions about machine-learned operators in general. CNO and CROP are evaluated only as corrective baselines and do not establish a general impossibility result.

The paper conflates discretization invariance with recovery of frequency content absent from the training distribution. Operator discretization convergence normally concerns evaluating the same underlying band-limited operator approximation on finer grids; it does not imply learning previously unseen Fourier modes. Labeling frequency extrapolation as a necessary component of zero-shot resolution transfer makes part of the negative result unsurprising and risks attacking a stronger claim than prior theory supports.

The FNO protocol is questionable. The authors advocate retaining all frequencies available at inference, even when corresponding Fourier weights could not have been trained on the coarse grid. Activating untrained modes at higher resolution can itself cause arbitrary artifacts. A decisive evaluation should compare against a standard fixed spectral cutoff and other discretization-consistent implementations under matched conditions.

The proposed solution has limited novelty: multi-resolution training is straightforward distribution coverage rather than zero-shot generalization, and related dual-resolution or active-learning approaches are already acknowledged. The paper does not provide an algorithm for choosing resolutions or sampling ratios.

The computational-efficiency claim is insufficiently supported. Average pixels per example is not total data-generation or training cost, dataset cardinalities and budget matching are unclear, and the reported mixtures are ambiguous—one listed tuple, (0.9, 0.5, 0.3, 0.2), does not define proportions summing to one. Wall-clock results are incomplete and do not establish end-to-end savings.

Several results weaken the stated conclusion. Figure 26 explicitly reports that CNO and CROP obtain lower Navier–Stokes losses than both FNO and multi-resolution training, while the text claims multi-resolution training is uniquely effective. Burgers also shows relatively small cross-resolution degradation in many settings. These qualifications are not reflected in the broad title and conclusions.

The spectral evidence does not convincingly establish aliasing in the signal-processing sense of frequency folding. Much of the evidence shows spurious high-frequency output, and normalized residuals can become enormous when divided by ground-truth energy that is near zero. Absolute spectral errors, explicit alias-frequency correspondence, and task-relevant normalized metrics are needed.

Experimental reliability and reproducibility are inadequate for the strength of the claims: no repeated runs, uncertainty estimates, train/validation/test sample counts, detailed architecture configurations, or released submission code are provided. Hyperparameters are tuned at only one resolution and reused elsewhere, and a CNO configuration fails to converge, raising concerns about baseline fairness.

The physics-informed comparison mainly demonstrates optimization failure, including worse in-distribution fitting. It does not justify the broader conclusion that physics constraints cannot enable multi-resolution generalization without stronger tuning, convergence controls, or comparisons to successful published configurations.

Overall, the work contains a useful cautionary empirical observation, but conceptual ambiguity, limited novelty, questionable protocol choices, contradictory baseline results, and incomplete statistical and computational validation keep it below the acceptance threshold.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and practically important question: whether mesh-invariant neural-operator architectures actually provide reliable zero-shot inference across discretizations.
The decomposition of multi-resolution inference into resolution interpolation and frequency-information extrapolation is conceptually useful and leads to informative diagnostic experiments.

The evaluation spans three PDE families, multiple train/test resolutions, spectral diagnostics, and comparisons with physics-informed and band-limited approaches. The observed aliasing and temporal compounding failures are practically significant.

Multi-resolution training is simple but useful, and the experiments suggest that mixing mostly inexpensive low-resolution samples with limited high-resolution data can provide a favorable accuracy-cost tradeoff.
The paper is generally well organized, and its figures communicate the principal failure modes effectively.
weaknesses: The central claims are substantially broader than the evidence. Most conclusions about machine-learned operators are based on FNO, while only CNO and CROP are considered as additional baselines. This does not establish a general limitation of MLOs.

The paper partially conflates discretization invariance with recovery of frequency content absent from training. Neural-operator resolution invariance is generally a consistency claim about approximating the same continuous operator, not a guarantee of reconstructing previously unobserved physical scales. The fixed-frequency interpolation experiment helps, but the framing and title remain stronger than justified.

Reproducibility is inadequate: dataset sample counts, train/validation/test splits, random seeds, number of independent runs, uncertainty estimates, detailed architecture configurations, preprocessing/downsampling procedures, and complete physics-loss implementations are missing. No code artifact is provided. One reported mixture, (0.9, 0.5, 0.3, 0.2), does not even form a valid proportion vector.

The evaluation reports essentially single-run averages without error bars or significance analysis. Spectral residuals normalized by ground-truth energy can strongly magnify errors where the denominator is very small, so raw spectral errors and aggregate relative norms are needed to establish practical importance.

The corrective-method comparisons are not fully convincing. Physics-informed models already underfit their training distribution, making their poor cross-resolution behavior weak evidence against physics-informed approaches in general. Loss-scale normalization and stronger optimization or weighting strategies are not investigated. Similarly, the CNO failure to converge on Burgers indicates an insufficiently resolved baseline.

Some results undermine the broad conclusions but are not discussed adequately: CNO and CROP outperform both FNO and multi-resolution training in Navier-Stokes MSE, despite the claim that multi-resolution training is the uniquely effective approach. The paper should distinguish spectral fidelity from task loss and explain which criterion matters operationally.

The proposed remedy has limited novelty: training on examples from each target resolution is an intuitive augmentation strategy closely related to prior multi-resolution active learning. Its main benefit is demonstrated only on a fixed, known set of four resolutions, without testing generalization to unseen intermediate resolutions or adaptive/nonuniform meshes.

The computational-efficiency claim relies largely on average pixel count and per-epoch time rather than an end-to-end accounting of data generation, training, memory, and accuracy-matched cost. Overall, the diagnostic study is promising, but these evaluation and reproducibility gaps place it marginally below the top-tier acceptance threshold.

strengths: Addresses an important practical question: whether discretization-invariant architectures actually provide accurate zero-shot inference across spatial resolutions.
The decomposition into resolution interpolation and frequency-information extrapolation is useful and motivates controlled spectral experiments.

The empirical study is unusually broad in several respects, covering Darcy, Burgers, and Navier–Stokes problems, multiple resolutions, FNO and limited DeepONet experiments, physics-informed objectives, band-limited methods, downsampling choices, and anti-aliasing nonlinearities.
The extensive appendix includes hyperparameter searches, spectral diagnostics, wall-clock measurements, a three-seed Darcy sensitivity study, and checks across computing architectures.
weaknesses: The central claims substantially exceed the evidence. Conclusions are repeatedly stated for machine-learned operators in general, but the main experiments concern one FNO implementation; DeepONet is tested only on Darcy, while other important operator-learning families are absent.

The proposed remedy—training on examples from every target resolution—is straightforward, closely related to cited multi-resolution and multi-fidelity training work, and turns the purported generalization problem largely into in-distribution learning. Its novelty and conceptual significance are therefore limited.

Most experiments appear to use a single seed. The three-seed analysis covers only Darcy and does not evaluate the proposed multi-resolution method or competing corrective methods, leaving the principal comparative claims without uncertainty estimates or significance analysis.

Baseline comparisons are not sufficiently controlled. Hyperparameters are tuned at one resolution and transferred elsewhere; CNO even fails to converge in one setting; physics-informed training is explored through a limited loss-weight grid; and parameter counts, optimization budgets, and effective training-data amounts are not matched. Poorly optimized baselines cannot establish that the corresponding approaches fundamentally fail.

The use of “aliasing” is technically imprecise. Excess high-frequency prediction energy or artifacts are evidence of spectral error, but not by themselves evidence of classical aliasing or frequency folding. The paper does not directly identify aliased frequency pairs or separate sampling aliasing from nonlinear spectral leakage and ordinary distribution shift.

The multi-resolution protocol is insufficiently specified: dataset sample counts, train/validation/test splits, batching of differently sized samples, and the precise meaning of ratios are missing. Reported tuples such as (0.9, 0.5, 0.3, 0.2) do not form proportions, despite being described as such, which makes the data and cost comparisons difficult to interpret or reproduce.

The computational-efficiency claim compares stored dataset size and training time against maximum-resolution training, but does not account convincingly for high-resolution simulation/data-generation cost or compare methods at a matched accuracy target. Burgers training time improves by only 3.2%.

There is an internal inconsistency in the Navier–Stokes band-limited evaluation: Figure 26 states that CNO and CROP obtain lower losses than both FNO and multi-resolution training, while the surrounding discussion broadly claims that these approaches underperform multi-resolution training.

Reproducibility remains limited because code is promised only after acceptance and important dataset and experimental details are absent. Overall, the paper offers useful negative empirical observations, but limited novelty, overbroad conclusions, and insufficiently controlled evidence prevent it from meeting the acceptance bar.

strengths: The paper studies an important practical question: whether neural operators remain accurate when evaluated at discretizations different from those used in training.
Separating resolution interpolation from frequency-information extrapolation is a useful diagnostic framing, and the spectral analyses expose artifacts that aggregate MSE alone could obscure.

Experiments cover three standard PDE datasets and examine several relevant interventions, including physics-informed losses, band-limited models, anti-aliased nonlinearities, alternative downsampling schemes, and multi-resolution training.
The appendix provides substantial implementation detail, hyperparameter searches, limited seed analysis, and measurements of memory and training-time tradeoffs.
weaknesses: The central framing conflates discretization invariance with recovery of genuinely unseen frequency content. A neural operator being evaluable on a finer grid does not imply that training on band-limited data should identify unconstrained high-frequency behavior. Consequently, the frequency-extrapolation failures are largely expected and do not by themselves refute the standard notion of discretization invariance.

The proposed remedy—training on examples at multiple resolutions—is straightforward and already represented in the cited multi-resolution, multi-fidelity, and active-learning literature. The paper offers neither a new algorithm for choosing resolutions nor a theoretical result, so the novelty is limited.

The claims about machine-learned operators are too broad. Most main experiments concern FNO; DeepONet is examined only on Darcy, while CNO and CROP are treated primarily as corrective baselines. This does not justify general conclusions about MLOs as a class.

Important controls are missing. In particular, the paper should compare against inference at the native training grid followed by principled spectral interpolation, and against carefully anti-aliased projection between grids. Strided downsampling can itself alias the underlying high-resolution fields, making different resolutions represent different discrete learning problems rather than clean samples of one continuous operator.

Comparisons with physics-informed and band-limited methods are not sufficiently conclusive. Physics-loss hyperparameters are selected at only one resolution per dataset and may require resolution-dependent normalization; band-limited methods are criticized for not predicting frequencies they deliberately exclude, which does not test their intended representation-equivalence guarantee.

Most headline results, including multi-resolution training and method comparisons, lack multi-seed uncertainty or statistical testing. Three-seed analysis is restricted to Darcy, while the more expensive Burgers and Navier–Stokes findings appear to rely on single runs.

The efficiency comparison does not fully control predictive accuracy, sample count, optimization budget, or data-generation cost. It mainly shows that storing and processing fewer high-resolution pixels is cheaper. Moreover, the repeatedly stated mixture (0.9, 0.5, 0.3, 0.2) does not sum to one and appears inconsistent with the plotted 90/5/3/2 mixture, impairing reproducibility.

The reported orders-of-magnitude variation in error across hardware/software stacks is alarming and insufficiently diagnosed. Deterministic forward predictions should not normally vary to this extent; attributing it generally to hardware without establishing numerical correctness weakens confidence in the implementation and conclusions.

The anonymous submission does not provide executable code, promising a link only upon acceptance, while some footnote links are blank. Together with unclear dataset counts, mixture definitions, and preprocessing details, this limits present reproducibility.

Overall, the paper documents a useful cautionary phenomenon, but its strongest conclusions overreach the evidence, the proposed solution has limited novelty, and several evaluation controls are needed before the work is competitive at a top-tier AI conference.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and practically relevant question: whether mesh-invariant neural operators actually provide accurate zero-shot inference across discretizations. The distinction between resolution interpolation and frequency-information extrapolation is useful and clarifies why architectural resolution flexibility does not guarantee numerical accuracy.

The empirical study is broad and carefully controlled. It covers Darcy flow, Burgers’ equation, and turbulent Navier–Stokes; evaluates super- and sub-resolution behavior; and includes spectral diagnostics that expose failures hidden by aggregate error metrics.

The conclusions are supported by substantial supplementary analysis, including maximum-mode ablations, alternative downsampling procedures, anti-aliasing nonlinearities, DeepONet experiments, three-seed sensitivity tests on Darcy, and comparisons across computing architectures.

The evaluation of proposed remedies is informative: physics-informed objectives, CNO, and CROP do not reliably recover unresolved spectral content, while multi-resolution training consistently improves performance.

The proposed training strategy is simple but useful. The experiments demonstrate favorable memory and training-time tradeoffs when datasets contain mostly inexpensive low-resolution samples and a small amount of high-resolution data.
The paper is clearly motivated, generally well organized, and likely to influence how neural-operator discretization-invariance claims are evaluated.
weaknesses: The central remedy—training on multiple resolutions—is intuitive and substantially overlaps prior multi-resolution, multi-fidelity, and active-learning work acknowledged by the authors. The main novelty is therefore the diagnostic study and synthesis rather than a new method.

Several conclusions are stated too broadly. Most comprehensive experiments concern FNO, while DeepONet and anti-aliasing variants are evaluated only on Darcy. Three PDE datasets from one benchmark are insufficient to establish that machine-learned operators generally cannot perform reliable zero-shot multi-resolution inference.

Statistical support is incomplete. Only the Darcy experiments are repeated across three seeds; the multi-resolution-training results, corrective-method comparisons, and larger Burgers and Navier–Stokes experiments appear to rely largely on single runs. Confidence intervals or paired statistical comparisons are absent.

Baseline fairness is not fully convincing. Hyperparameters are tuned at only one resolution per dataset and transferred to other resolutions, CNO fails to converge in one important setting, and the physics-informed loss implementation is described only at a high level. Per-method and per-resolution tuning or stronger convergence checks could materially affect comparisons.

Reproducibility is weaker than the extensive appendix suggests: code is promised only after acceptance, dataset split sizes and sampling counts are not clearly reported, and the precise construction and normalization of multi-resolution mixture ratios are insufficiently explicit.

The paper sometimes conflates several phenomena under the term “aliasing,” including ordinary out-of-distribution prediction error and spurious high-frequency energy. A more precise separation of sampling aliasing, nonlinear architectural aliasing, and distribution shift would strengthen the technical claims.

Presentation needs polishing: there are numerous typographical errors and ambiguous ratio notation, while some captions are inconsistent with their plots—for example, the axes described for the hardware-comparison figure appear reversed. Several appendix figures are also too dense for easy interpretation.
